title: "La Presidenza italiana dell'Unione Europea" - org. dall'Istituto Affari Internazionali e dal TEPSA (Trans European Policy Studies Association con il sostegno del Ministero per gli Affari Esteri, la Commissione Europea e la Compagnia di San Paolo  (presso
text: senso intorno ad ipotesi di questo tipo e quindi è un semestre e una sfida difficile per il nostro Paese. Oggi quindi la nostra conferenza inizia con questo tema prioritario, la Costituzione. Domani invece dedicheremo i nostri lavori alla politica estera, che è un altro tema fondamentale e divideremo i lavori in gruppi sui Balcani, sul Mediterraneo, sulla Russia, sull'Iraq, che sono punti di grande interesse per l'Italia e per l'Unione Europea, ma che sono anche legati strettamente alla richiesta di riforma della Costituzione, e cioè in altre parole al rafforzamento di quel ruolo di politica estera e di sicurezza che è necessario perché l'Unione Europea giochi un ruolo importante internazionale. Quindi diciamo che queste due parti della nostra conferenza sono legate a filo doppio proprio per la logica con cui si tengono assieme una riforma istituzionale che di fatto crea questa capacità europea di agire come attore internazionale. Ecco, di fronte con queste considerazioni, io volei naturalmente ringraziare anche gli sponsor di questa nostra iniziativa, la Commissione di Bruxelles, la Compagnia di San Paolo, ma soprattutto il Ministero degli Esteri, che ci ha seguito molto, è qui rappresentato fra il resto da Ferdinando Nelli-Feroci, con cui abbiamo confezionato, diciamo, questa conferenza. E un grazie anche al circolo ufficiali, Palazzo Barberini, che ci ha ospitato per il calore con cui ci ha accolto, proprio in merito mi è tolto le parole. Grazie e passo la parola in ordine alfabetico, seguiamo, ma anche in ordine siccome gerarchico, perché come vicepresidente della Convenzione chiederei a Giuliano Matto di aprire la discussione. Grazie. Quanti minuti? 19 minuti. Ok, well, substantially Gianni, you said what has to be said. It's not perfect, the draft that we have produced is not perfect. I wonder if the Intergovernmental Conference is equipped to improve it or to worsen it. And I frankly think that they might more easily worsen it than improve it, which means that the shortcomings of the existing text are doomed to remain in my view. I'm very pessimistic on this, because I sound and their positions of national governments ready to do something in terms of changing what has been done and what they have in mind to change is on the wrong side. Of course, worsening or improving depends on what you think. Let's say in my view, in my view I'm firmly convinced to pick one point that giving each of our member states a commissioner with full rights is not an improvement. I understand that the commission, for reasons that frankly I don't share, has a different position. But in my view, in my view, there is a limit to the efficiency of the commission that doesn't go beyond a certain number of commissioners holding a portfolio without slicing the existing portfolios into pieces that requires the commission not to go beyond something that is around 15 full members. And this was exactly what not Giscard but Jacques Delors advised us to do. Now, let me state this point. In our view, let's say human beings may be part of the structure. Only 15 full members of it, but other commissioners coming from other countries can be appointed and can be useful as long as they are something such as delegated commissioners. When people say, well, there are so many national governments with 30, 40 ministers, the French government is quoted as a government having 40 ministers, but at this point any French who knows how things are in his or her country objects, but only 15 are full ministers, the other are delegated ministers. And this is what we expect the commission to be. Consider that initially we called, we named the other commissioners, delegated commissioners. I made a negotiation with the national governments in the convention. They accepted, they accepted all of them, all of them, 15 full members on a strictly equal rotation basis. At that point they asked me to give the others a name that they could sell in their countries. And it was not a matter of selling, not a matter of substance. And they objected to the delegated commissioner because it seemed something more hierarchically subordinated than something else. And therefore at the end we called the first class commissioners European commissioners and the other ones commissioners. At this point there are reactions in some countries and they say, but what are these gentlemen going to do hanging around? They are not even delegated to do something. Now the response is read the draft and the draft says that the president of the commission is responsible toward the European Parliament for the activities of these commissioners, which means that the president will give them missions to each of them and he or she will be responsible for their activities toward the parliament. It is, I must say at the end of the story, the same kind of commission that the commission had in mind, the two tiers commission, which means that in a two tiers commission not necessarily all of them have the voting rights around. Now this is a crucial point in my view. I am convinced that with the commission having at the end of the story more than 30 full members with voting rights the commission would become an intergovernmental arena, somehow reducing its potential as the necessary engine in the European interest. For several member states changing the draft in this sense would be improving it. So we have to be very clear on what we consider improving or worsening. I can expect this kind of thing to have quite a significant pressure during the intergovernmental conference, which would be a pity because the commission has been strengthened throughout the process. I must say I am one of those who have always thought that a long term president is useful for the council. So let's say Herman is one that was opposing it and wanted the prize for it. So if I have to swallow the president, this is Herman's argument, what do you give me? And he got something because he got for the commission significant improvement in terms of tasks, not just the monopoly in legislative initiative, not just the almost monopoly in executive functions, but also the yearly and multi yearly planning of union activities which is going to be organized on the basis of the commission initiative, plus the European council meetings jointly prepared by the general affairs council and by the commission, plus at the end the president of the commission jointly with the president of the council supervising the preparation of the European council and also the elimination of that clause by which there was an incompatibility between the presidency of the European council and the presidency of the commission, which is much less than the clause some of us had in mind to give the union a single president in let's say 10 years, but at least it opens the way to it. Therefore the commission is somehow safe in its role and the institutional balance has been preserved, but should the arena I was envisaging this in my view would be a significant worsening in the future of the institutional balance itself. Qualified majority, I don't think the IGC will do something to widen the cases of qualified majority indeed. I don't think the IGC will do something to widen the cases of qualified majority. At the end of the story there are some cases, substantially some cases and you have several governments playing against here or there. Taxation distorting competition could be somehow decided upon by qualified majority voting, but you don't have the UK only, you also have Denmark, you also have Ireland, you also have Sweden, you also have others. Social policies, it's not the UK, it's Germany that is firmly opposing qualified majority in relation to the now Article 137 and they don't want to go beyond Nice. France is already resenting the limited ventilation that we introduced in agricultural policy, giving something to legislation and much more to Council's regulations. I have already seen amendments that reduce the something given to European legislation and should this amendment be accepted sooner or later, legislation would just have the smoke and all of the meat would be and would remain for Council's regulation. What can I expect from the IGC that France drops its objections to widening the role of qualified majority and co-decision in agricultural policy in exchange for Germany widening the area of social policies that go to co-decision and qualified majority? This is something unpredictable and therefore to conclude with, I don't think that there will be leftovers formally, I am convinced that there will be leftovers substantially, so I don't expect the IGC to formally decide that unsettled issue will go to a further appointment with either a Convention or an IGC. I expect them to remain where we have remained if not worse in this area. I include in this area also amendments of the text because you are right Gianni, it would be so reasonable and this was something that Herman and I proposed jointly, we accept unanimity for any amendment that imply further transfers of sovereignty from member states to the Union, while any other amendment which simply implies reorganisation at the European level of existing competences and therefore does not reduce or touch upon what remains in the hands of member states, why shouldn't this be approved by a majority vote? Possibly by a super qualified majority voting, what's the reason? Really there is no reason, I ignore now the fact that they want the procedure of international treaties to apply also for the future therefore not the European Council but the IGC, not the national parliaments approving but the national parliaments ratifying which is really something that for me as a lawyer means treaty, cannot mean constitution but independently also of it, why don't they accept majority voting when their remaining competences are not touched upon by the amendments? The funny thing is that at the end of this process, this one, we might find ourselves with an overall more cumbersome procedure for amendments than the existing one because nowadays we have several clauses that can be modified by quasi autonomous or autonomous procedures and as we say in technical jargon by which national parliaments are not involved, unanimity is necessary anyway but the unanimity of the European Council could be enough now to change several clauses of the existing treaties. Paradoxically you understand how times change, one of the clauses that can be changed only by decision of the European Council without involving national parliaments is the clause on the number of commissioners that has become the hottest issue of the European Council of all, so I don't expect this to change, what do I expect? I do expect in a few years the union to face some deep crisis because they cannot decide on the basis of unanimity. Assuming unanimity as the method for their decisions, the European Council simply means that they cannot decide even more in an enlarged Europe and therefore after a while they will realize perhaps by themselves that if they really want to exercise the competencies they wanted at the European level but unanimously decided upon, they will have to change. In the last three months of the convention this was not even mentioned anymore by national parliaments because it was thought that this was a positive result which will help us in the future to come to a good relationship between national parliaments and European parliaments in order to fulfill our responsibility to control the executive branches. Thank you very much. Thank you, Elmer Brock, for your evaluation of the result of the convention and also for your sharp judgment on the role of the IGC. In any case, may I now, before addressing to the audience and ask for some questions or comments, may I ask Ferdinando Nell'Efferoci to comment about this first round of introductions without anticipating the priorities of the Italian presidencies which will be part of the next session. Thank you. Gianni, thank you. I think I can limit my remarks to very brief ones because I'd like to say a little more on how we would like to proceed in the preparation of the IGC and in the conduct of the IGC in fact. Broadly speaking, I'd like to confirm what has already been said at official level by several representatives of the Italian government including Vice President Fini who has been an active member of the convention, including Presidente Berlusconi, including Foreign Minister Mr. Flattini, and this is to confirm that we really very much appreciate the results achieved by the convention. We think that we are in the presence of a historical development. If we look back into the past way of proceeding in treaty reforms and treaty revisions, we are now faced with an extraordinary crisis of innovation and we are also very much satisfied with the overall articulation of the draft constitutional treaty which has been submitted to the government in Tessaloniki. Maybe as many others, members of parliaments, representatives of governments, we would have had preferences here and there. There would have been solutions that we would like to see more than others reflected in the draft treaty, but as a whole we consider that it's a very good basis for the work of the intergovernmental conference. I fully share the appreciation which was made a few minutes ago by Presidente Amato when he noted that there is a risk in reopening the carefully balanced text of the treaty dispositions and the risk is that we may fall backwards more than move forwards. We would carefully study all the alternatives that we will be faced with when launching the IGC, but certainly we will carefully have in mind this note of caution. In more general terms, I think that I fully share the individual points that were made by President Brock and that all together we share his points of appreciation for the text. But having said that, I think I would prefer to leave it for my next intervention, some more detailed remarks on how we intend to proceed further on on our way towards the organization of the intergovernmental conference. Thank you, Alvaro. Ok, thank you very much. Now I address to the audience for questions and comments. Of course there is a mobile phone. Yes, please, could you come here? Alvaro de Vasconcelos from the Instituto de Estudios Strategicos of Lisbon. Yes, thank you very much. I want to make a comment and put a question to the panel. The comment is that I have the feeling that there was real progress in making the European integration more democratic, more transparent, more close to the citizens. Let's say if you look from outside, in Europe we are better now. Integration is moving forward. My question is the following. If this is true for Europe, it's not the same thing in relation to the ability of the European Union to project its values in the international scene. It's clear about what you said, but also just reading the constitution, that even the premise that came from the convention are not in this text. We have no majority voting as it was proposed in the Franco-German proposal. On the fence there is not really great progress. We don't have a clause of solidarity, clear clause of solidarity. So we have not really progressed on the ability to act internationally. So now coming to the question, is this the lessons you took from the Iraqi crisis? You spoke as a parliamentarian, I spoke as a citizen. And looking to your work, I ask myself, have you done your work based on the Iraqi crisis to make the European Union more able to act internationally? Or it was just the opposite, that the Iraq crisis made you more timid, less able to make the reform that was asked? Because looking to the debate in the convention and the result, it seems that there is two moments. Before the Iraq crisis, things seemed to go forward on the foreign policy and defense. And after the Iraq crisis, to opposite to the Iraq crisis, we have no lessons of Europeans in the streets that ask for more Europe in the demonstrations all over Europe. We don't have that. More Europe in international affairs. And it's a demand from outside Europe too. It's not only in Europe. If we go to North Africa, to the Middle East, to Latin America, to Africa, people say we need more Europe, not less Europe in the international arena. Why it is not there? Thank you. May I suggest to collect some questions and comments and then go back to the panel? I have another person there. Can you introduce yourself, please? My name is Rafał Trzaskowski. I'm from the European Center in Poland and I have a question to Mr. Edmund Brock. You have said that what parliamentarians achieved shouldn't change, have no right to change, and it's very difficult to disagree with that statement. But wouldn't you agree that hadn't there been an IGC plan, the achievements of the convention wouldn't be so far reaching? In other words, if you talk to many of the participants of the convention, parliamentarians included, some of them are not satisfied with the draft treaty. And so it seems that some of them have adopted a strategy, let's not spoil the celebration and let's wait for the IGC to change certain things that we don't like. You have said that there will be no big changes during the IGC. What changes do you envisage, if any? Thank you. Thank you. Other questions? We have a very timid audience here, not the convention, but the audience. Please. Yes, please. Dominik Hanf from the College of Europe in Bruges. This one? Yeah, okay. My question is concerning the adoption of the new constitution. All these matters on the adoption and the later revision of the constitution by a qualified majority have not really been discussed, but there will be a problem of fact that what will happen if one or two or three member states will not adopt the new constitution. So I know that the treaty, or the draft treaty, will have a problem and take political consequences, but my question is what will be the political consequences? Okay, thank you. Another question here and then there. The question is the following. Your name, please, to introduce yourself. Sorry, my name is Jan Willems. I'm the Belgian ambassador to the Quid Inan here in Rome. Why did the convention not suggest to the IGC that the end result, the constitution, would enter into force with less than a new unanimous ratification in the different member states? Because we can face the result and the risk is greater that one country would block the entry into force of this new constitution, which would be tragic. Thank you very much, Ambassador. Another question there. My name is Brendan Donnelly from the Federal Trust in London. Can I put a question arising from what Elmar Brock said about foreign policy, but I'd like comments if I may from everyone on that subject. Elmar Brock spoke as if the most important reason why a relatively cautious text on the question of foreign policy emerged was British opposition. It's widely believed in the United Kingdom, and I'd like a comment on this if I may, that while the British government is the most outspoken in its opposition to a more daring approach to foreign policy, in fact at least the French government and in some moods the German government has more sympathy with that view than is always publicly said. Now, whether that's right or wrong, can I just make the further point that British public and probably British elite opinion will never be convinced of any different proposition until what Elmar said was a possibility does happen. If you want to convince the British that they're the only people who are standing in the way of a more bold foreign policy, then it's up to others to take the lead. Other questions? Yes, please. General Pozzi, retired from the Italian Army, member of the Istituto D'Affari Internazionali. What about the security and defense? What will be the provisions in that sector? I would like to know if it is, of course, is in the agenda, but what ideas are going to be in the agenda that will be constructed in the end? Thank you. Thank you. Other questions? Questions can be also addressed in Italian. I'm Paolo Calzini of Milano University. How do you assess the fact that there has been so little debate and participation in terms of public opinion in Europe around the question of the Constitution? Thank you. Okay. I would suggest to go back to the two main speakers and ask them to answer or to comment or to conclude their reasoning here by thanking them, of course, for their patience and having succeeded to resist this hot climate. Please. Well, first of all, when you say that public opinion was somehow far from the Convention, you say something that is only partially true and much less than you think. First, you have to compare the attention given by public opinion to the Convention with the attention given to IGCs, because this is the only alternative, the benchmark. For the first time, if you look at this from this angle, we had an enormous debate compared with the past, a transparent debate that we never had in the past on modifications of the treaties. Please give a look at the side of the Convention and give a look at that part of the side that is named Forum. Under Forum, you have all the associations, groups and centers of research and others that took part in the debate by sending contribution, by interacting with us, by taking part in meetings, because we also had meetings with the representatives of this group. They are hundreds and hundreds, and not just the traditional lobbies that are based in Brussels and that of course show up whatever happens in Brussels, but also associations and groups from all the existing member states and the new member states. Some of them, unbelievable, because I did never expect the association for the safeguard of the right to nudity to have something to suggest, which if they suggested something, nothing appeared in the text, I suppose, except I hope the Charter takes care also of nudity, I don't know. But anyhow, there was quite an attention, so please don't say as usual, well, the citizens were absent. This is not correct. I don't expect the attention of let's say millions and millions of people to go to an event such as the Convention. I expect those citizens who tend to be active to have an opportunity to interact, to have a sense of responsibility, to have a sense of responsibility
